selectionSummary: Consistent world-impact criterion: cross-border reach, scale of human consequences, international-security and climate-system effects, independently verified breadth of reporting and durable institutional implications. Selected three distinct developments: unprecedented nuclear-power summit, historic genocide judgment and COP31 draft negotiation.

snapshot.summary: On November 19, formal statements and judicial findings highlighted the gap between promises and implementation: three powers made modest peace commitments, a court imposed binding accountability without direct enforcement, and climate negotiators debated a draft stripped of fossil-fuel language.
connections: Each story tests the reach of international institutions: the UN and international courts, the ICJ Genocide Convention, and the UN climate process.
The summit declaration mentioned legal immunities on the same day an international court ruled on state responsibility; this coincidence does not establish causation.
All three distinguish official words or legal decisions from concrete, enforceable consequences.
uncertainties: Whether summit pledges would yield actual nuclear or peace arrangements.
Whether Myanmar would implement binding reparations and safe return.
Whether COP31 would agree a final text or restore explicit fossil-fuel commitments.

stories.title: US, Chinese and Russian leaders sign limited Shenzhen declaration
stories.summary: The first Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral summit produced a four-part declaration about UN reform, petroleum supply, state official immunity and future nuclear-risk dialogue. The public text did not resolve the wars in Ukraine and Iran or establish a new nuclear arms agreement.
stories.whyItMatters: The three countries' strategic arsenals, influence over global institutions and roles in existing wars make their commitments consequential far beyond Asia.
stories.selectionRationale: Great-power nuclear security, cross-border war diplomacy and potential changes to international institutions; directly reported by multiple independent newsrooms.
stories.evidenceNote: AP original report, original Xinhua Xi remarks and original Guardian Shenzhen dispatch were opened. Xi's assessment of success is attributed; a declaration is not implementation.

articles.summary: After roughly 70 minutes, the leaders announced cooperation on UN reform, oil refining, ICC jurisdiction and nuclear-risk dialogue without resolving the Iran or Ukraine wars.

commonFacts.text: Trump, Xi and Putin held trilateral talks in Shenzhen on November 19.
The limited declaration covered the UN, refined oil supply, official immunity and nuclear-risk dialogue; it did not promise an end to either major war.
Xi publicly called the talks constructive; the assessment was made while the concrete measures remained modest.

framingDifferences.text: DISPUTED QUESTION: Was the meeting an effective contribution to global peace, or primarily symbolic major-power diplomacy that left those affected by wars outside the room? POSITION A: Xi, reported by Xinhua, called it fruitful and said the three countries recognized the need to respect every state's security concerns. POSITION B: European critics and the Guardian's account stress that Ukraine and Iran were omitted from the declaration and no settlement was secured. EVIDENCE: AP independently reports both the declaration and lack of a substantive breakthrough; Xi's assertion of peace benefits remains an attributed judgment.
All sources concur the summit and declaration occurred; the material disagreement is whether diplomatic contact and broad principles suffice as real progress, not whether the leaders met.

uncertainties: Whether nuclear-risk discussions would become enforceable arms-control limits.
Whether peace diplomacy would include the states and populations directly affected.
Whether the oil, ICC and UN positions would have policy consequences.

unverifiedClaims.text: Xi called the summit fruitful for global peace.
unverifiedClaims.reason: A political interpretation, not independently measurable proof of peace.

unverifiedClaims.text: Trump described the summit as historic and suggested it advanced a Ukraine settlement.
unverifiedClaims.reason: No peace agreement was signed by cutoff.

stories.title: UN court holds Myanmar responsible for genocide against Rohingya
stories.summary: The International Court of Justice ruled 9-6 that Myanmar's 2017 military campaign committed genocide against the Rohingya population. The majority rejected Myanmar's argument that counterinsurgency alone explained the violence and ordered remedies including safe return and compensation, whose implementation remains unresolved.
stories.whyItMatters: The ICJ's first judgment holding a state responsible for genocide establishes a landmark precedent, while more than a million displaced Rohingya remain exposed to continuing insecurity.
stories.selectionRationale: Exceptional legal precedent, large-scale displacement, human rights significance and consequences for state accountability in other cases.
stories.evidenceNote: Reuters and Guardian cover the delivered court ruling; an earlier Al Jazeera original explainer specifically documents Myanmar's disputed defense before it was rejected. No later political outcome is assumed.

lens.rationale: Kaamil Ahmed and Oliver Holmes report judges' conclusion of genocidal intent, including killings, sexual violence and measures preventing births.

articles.summary: The ICJ's nine-judge majority concluded the 2017 operations intended to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population, rejecting Myanmar's counterterrorism explanation.

provenance.evidenceNote: Guardian staff Kaamil Ahmed and Oliver Holmes; first published 12:08 CET=11:08 UTC, updated 14:52 CET Nov19, within cutoff.

commonFacts.text: A 9-6 ICJ majority found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya in the 2017 campaign.
Myanmar's defense asserted a counterterrorism rationale and denied genocidal intent; Gambia submitted the opposite case.
The court ordered redress and provision for safe return but lacked a means to enforce compliance directly.

framingDifferences.text: DISPUTED QUESTION: Did the military operation amount to intentional destruction of the Rohingya, or justified counterinsurgency against armed groups? POSITION A: Myanmar's representatives, reported by Al Jazeera in a pre-judgment explainer, argued security necessity and denied genocidal intent; this is an actor's position, not the newsroom's endorsement. POSITION B: The ICJ majority, reported by the Guardian, ruled that widespread killings, sexual violence and other acts established an intent to destroy part of the group, rejecting that explanation. EVIDENCE: Reuters independently details the delivered binding judgment; the judicial finding has decisive legal weight over the rejected position, not equal evidentiary weight.

Pre-verdict and post-verdict sources reflect the same legal dispute at different stages, not contradicting newsrooms. The judgment established legal state responsibility, not actual enforcement or individuals' criminal convictions.

uncertainties: How Myanmar would respond to binding reparations and non-repetition obligations.
Whether refugees could ever return voluntarily with security and rights guaranteed.
Whether international enforcement or individual criminal proceedings would follow.

unverifiedClaims.text: Myanmar argued the 2017 operation was counterinsurgency without genocidal intent.
unverifiedClaims.reason: Attribution of an ultimately rejected legal defense, not evidence that genocide did not occur.

unverifiedClaims.text: Supporters hoped the verdict would enable safe repatriation.
unverifiedClaims.reason: An expected benefit, not a completed return or enforced reparation.

stories.title: COP31 draft drops fossil-fuel commitments as deadline approaches
stories.summary: The November 19 draft of COP31's Antalya Declaration removed language on ending fossil fuel use and softened electrification commitments. Turkey and Australia defended an achievable package to implement existing climate goals. Campaigners and vulnerable countries demanded stronger fossil-fuel and climate-finance terms; no final agreement was confirmed by the Paris cutoff.
stories.whyItMatters: Nearly 200 countries' climate policy signals guide emissions, clean-energy investment and the resources available to populations facing the greatest climate risks.
stories.selectionRationale: Long-term worldwide climate, health, finance and energy investment consequences with directly conflicting negotiated prescriptions.
stories.evidenceNote: Reuters checked the wording; Anadolu original interviews/briefing explain presidency case; Guardian independently covers criticism. Guardian was modified after cutoff, so only corroborated Nov19 draft facts were used.

commonFacts.text: A Nov19 second draft excluded fossil-fuel phaseout language and softened electrification wording.
The presidency continued promoting a proposed 35% electricity share of global final energy use by 2035.
The draft was still under negotiation as the deadline approached, with disagreement over finance and fossil-fuel language.

framingDifferences.text: DISPUTED QUESTION: Should negotiators retain clear fossil-fuel transition and ambitious finance language even at the risk of no consensus, or prioritize an adoptable implementation package? POSITION A: COP president Murat Kurum, described in original Anadolu reporting, defended a concrete implementation approach centered on electrification and adaptation. POSITION B: Campaigners and Panama, quoted by the Guardian, said the omissions undermined the climate goal and demanded tougher wording. EVIDENCE: Reuters corroborates the changed draft, not promised emissions reductions or the forecast of a failed summit.

The sources agree the draft was weakened and unfinished; the opposed positions concern whether pragmatic political compromise is adequate climate action or an unacceptable retreat, not different time definitions.

uncertainties: Whether final text would restore any fossil-fuel phaseout commitment.
Whether developed countries would agree stronger quantified adaptation finance.
Whether a 35% electrification goal would be adopted and depend on renewable power.

unverifiedClaims.text: The Turkish presidency said electrification and adaptation would make the draft a practical Paris-aligned success.
unverifiedClaims.reason: An advocacy and implementation projection, not accomplished emissions cuts.

unverifiedClaims.text: Campaigners warned the weak wording risked making COP31 a symbolic failure.
unverifiedClaims.reason: An attributed prediction before the final conference decision.
